extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of literary and military history
extracted.subtask_description: A nonfiction narrative account and critique of the Spanish–American War focusing on preparation, conduct, and consequences of military operations. Emphasizes causes of success/failure in army and navy performance and public/administrative factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naval professionalism and readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The navy was a fully professional arm, ready for action both in equipment and in plans, and able to take a prompt initiative in carrying out an aggressive campaign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative emphasis on professional preparation: correct equipment, pre-existing plans, and capacity for prompt initiative; contrasted repeatedly with army shortcomings as an explanation for naval success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational secrecy and press discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The activity of the American press revealed the navy's and army's every move; press boats and correspondents frequently compromised operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes reporters for acting as part of the army and disclosing plans (e.g., blazoning Lieutenant Whitney's spy plans), and highlights Admiral Sampson's request for secrecy as a necessary practice that was largely honored — except for dangerous exceptions. Operational security and controlled press access are presented as essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and use of a general staff / professional planning
rubrics_metrics.description: There existed no general staff to advise the Secretary of War; absence of a staff contributed to poor Army administration and strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author faults the War Department and Secretary Alger for not creating or consulting a general staff, implying that systematic professional advisory structures are a requisite for competent military administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officer training and professional military education
rubrics_metrics.description: West Point and Annapolis provided college courses, but in the army there was 'no provision for systematic graduate study corresponding to the Naval War College at Newport.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative asserts that lack of advanced/professional education and failure to sift ability before appointments left many officers unprepared for modern warfare; recommends institutional graduate-level instruction and selection by merit rather than seniority or politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate selection and appointment of commanders
rubrics_metrics.description: Many high appointments were sentimental or political (e.g., elderly ex-Confederate generals), resulting in commanders physically or mentally unfit for tropical campaign demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appointments should favor current competence and fitness for the specific operational environment rather than political patronage or past service; the text cites Shafter's frailty and the impropriety of some political selections as causes of failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-deployment officer training for volunteers
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers raised for the volunteer army were largely amateur and 'given no officer training whatsoever but was turned directly to the task of training the rank and file.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Volunteer and new officers need preparatory officer training before being assigned command responsibilities; skipping this step degrades unit effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate logistics: munitions and transport infrastructure
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular belief that wealth alone could substitute for logistical planning blinded people to the lack of transport facilities (single track to Tampa) and munitions readiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material resources must be matched by transport infrastructure and explicit logistical planning; assumptions that ingenuity/wealth will compensate are criticized as dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communications and modern equipment
rubrics_metrics.description: The want of means of communication paralyzed the command: there were no aeroplanes, no wireless stations, no telephones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern communications and reconnaissance technologies (then-current: balloons, wireless, telephones; now analogous modern systems) are essential; absence cripples command and control and risks unnecessary casualties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical preparation, sanitation, and disease prevention
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary cause for the melting of the American army by disease must be acknowledged to be the insufficient training of the officers; commanders had not recognized the mosquito as the carrier of yellow fever or seen the need for inoculation against typhoid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-deployment medical knowledge (disease vectors, inoculations), quarantine measures, adequate surgeons and hospital services, and climate-appropriate clothing are vital to preserve force strength; failure produced catastrophic illness and death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate clothing and rations for climate
rubrics_metrics.description: There was no excuse for sending many of the men clad in heavy army woolens or for failing to investigate proper rations for use in the tropics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisioning (clothing, rations) must fit the operational environment; adherence to domestic standards without adaptation to climate is negligent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and seasonality of operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Sending an expedition from the United States to the tropics in midsummer when measures necessary to safeguard health were not yet known was irresponsible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing of campaigns must take into account climatic/disease seasons and provide delay if necessary to prepare protective measures; political impatience should not override operational prudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate medical staffing and hospital service
rubrics_metrics.description: There was no excuse for not providing a sufficient number of surgeons and abundant hospital service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medical personnel and facilities must be scaled to expedition size and expected disease burden; lack thereof contributed to high morbidity/mortality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational planning and task assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: The blockade was 'systematically planned' with each American ship having its definite place and particular duty; coaling rotations were covered by relief ships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear allocation of roles, contingency coverage (e.g., while vessels coal), and systematic scheduling are cited as hallmarks of effective operations and contrasted with ad hoc army practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of initiative and enlistment of individual initiative
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite organizational shortcomings, the American victory owed much to the fighting spirit of the men and to the individual initiative of line and field officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individual courage and initiative are important force multipliers, especially when systemic deficiencies exist, but should not be relied upon as a substitute for sound organization and planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilian leadership competence and seeking professional advice
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary defect was at the top: Secretary Alger did not understand the functions of his office, did not seek professional advice, and even forbade spending of defense funds in ways that hampered operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civilian leaders must understand their responsibilities, consult professionals, and enable proper spending and contracting; political priorities must not obstruct operational needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of political patronage in military administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Indolence of Secretary Alger and his 'worship of politics' produced many secondary errors (embalmed beef controversy, inappropriate appointments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative decisions should minimize political favoritism; technical and logistical choices must be made on professional grounds to avoid harmful outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative diplomatic/political solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of War's unconventional offer to transport Spanish troops at once and without parole in return for unconditional surrender was politically effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flexible, politically aware solutions can achieve military/diplomatic goals; creativity in negotiation and policy can produce pragmatic results when conventional options are limited.
